title: Building the Database
text:
Methodology


This project reconstructs the lives of Chinese men who served in the American Civil War by tracing their presence across a fragmented and uneven archival record. Rather than relying on a single source base, it brings together military records, census data, pension files, newspapers, and genealogical databases to identify individuals and follow them across time.


Reconstructing a Fragmented Archive


Chinese individuals in the nineteenth-century United States often appear only intermittently in official records. Their lives are preserved not in continuous narratives, but in scattered references across different types of documents. As a result, reconstructing these histories requires working across gaps, inconsistencies, and absences in the archive.


This project treats fragmentation not simply as a limitation, but as a central feature of the historical record. The difficulty of tracing these men reflects the broader conditions under which Chinese lives were documented, categorized, and often marginalized in nineteenth-century American institutions.


Identifying the Soldiers


The first step in building this project involved identifying Chinese or Chinese-born individuals within Civil War military and naval records. This process began with enlistment records, particularly naval rendezvous records and service registers, which provided names, ages, places of birth, and dates of service.


From these initial entries, individuals were traced across additional sources, including federal census schedules, pension files, newspaper articles, and genealogical databases such as FamilySearch, Ancestry, and FindAGrave. Digital collections such as the National Archives Catalog and Fold3 were also central to this process.


Cross-Referencing Records


Because no single record provides a complete account of an individual’s life, this project relies on cross-referencing multiple sources to confirm identities and reconstruct life histories. A single individual might appear under slightly different names or spellings in different records, requiring comparison across age, birthplace, service history, occupation, and family connections.


For example, a naval enlistment record might provide a name, age, and place of birth, while a later census record offers information about residence, occupation, and household structure. Pension files and newspaper coverage can further extend these narratives, providing evidence of postwar life, health, and social connections.


This method allows for the reconstruction of individual lives even when no single source contains a complete account. Instead, meaning emerges through the accumulation and alignment of multiple partial records.


Limits and Uncertainty


Despite these efforts, significant gaps remain. Many individuals appear only briefly in the historical record, and some cannot be traced beyond a single document. Names are frequently misspelled or altered, and racial identification is inconsistent across sources. These limitations make it difficult to confirm identities with absolute certainty in every case.


Rather than attempting to resolve all ambiguities, this project acknowledges uncertainty as part of the historical process. The gaps in the archive are not simply obstacles, but evidence of how Chinese lives were recorded, categorized, and sometimes excluded from official narratives.


Building the Database


The individuals identified through this process were compiled into a working database that records key details such as name, birthplace, age, military branch, rank, service dates, and postwar life events when available. This database serves as the foundation for both the soldier profiles and the broader thematic analysis presented throughout the site.


By combining quantitative organization with qualitative interpretation, the project moves between individual lives and larger historical questions about race, military service, migration, and belonging in the nineteenth-century United States.


These methods can be seen in practice in the individual soldier profiles, where fragmented records are brought together to reconstruct individual lives.

title: Race and Recognition
text:
How did military service make Chinese men visible within a system that often excluded them? During the Civil War era, the act of enlistment entered them into bureaucratic systems that recorded, categorized, and, in some cases, fixed their identities within official state structures.


Race and Bureaucratic Systems


In nineteenth-century America, race was not only a social category but also an administrative one. Government institutions relied on documentation—enlistment papers, service records, census schedules, and pension files—to classify individuals and organize populations. These systems translated lived identities into standardized categories that could be recorded and managed.


For Chinese men, this process was uneven and often inconsistent. Racial identification could shift depending on the context, the recorder, or the purpose of the document. At the same time, the very act of being recorded placed these men within official systems that might otherwise have overlooked or excluded them.




(left) Hong Neok Woo c. 1860 in Lancaster, PA. From the Collections of LancasterHistory. (right) Corporal Joseph Pierce of Co. F 14th Connecticut Infantry Regiment. Liljenquist Family Collection.



Military Records as Sites of Recognition


Military service created new opportunities for Chinese men to enter these bureaucratic systems. Enlistment records required the documentation of key details such as name, age, place of birth, and occupation. Service records and muster rolls extended this documentation across time, while pension files could preserve information decades after the war.



Muster Roll for Antonio Dardelle, National Archives and Records Administration (Washington D.C.), National Archives Catalog, <https://catalog.archives.gov/id/146919982?objectPage=5>.





John Wylee Rendezvous Report, 1862. U.S. National Archives and Records Administration. “Wylee, John.” Index to Rendezvous Reports, Civil War, 1861–1865. Accessed via Fold3. <https://www.fold3.com/image/310113356.>



These records helped produce an identity. By assigning names, categories, and descriptors to individuals, military documentation contributed to the process of making Chinese men legible to the state. In this way, the military functioned not only as a site of labor and service, but also as a site of recognition and classification.


Individual Records and Archival Traces


The impact of this process can be seen in the surviving records of individual soldiers. The extensive documentation connected to John (Ah) Hang, including his pension file and later interview, provides a rare example of how bureaucratic systems could preserve a detailed account of a Chinese life across multiple decades.


Recognition and Its Limits


Despite this increased visibility, recognition within bureaucratic systems did not guarantee broader social or legal inclusion. Chinese men who served in the military were still subject to exclusionary laws, racial discrimination, and shifting definitions of citizenship. Being recorded did not necessarily mean being accepted.




“Kwong Lee was shot five times in the defense of the country of which he was not yet a citizen.” The San Francisco Call, July 23, 1909.



At the same time, the existence of these records complicates narratives of complete exclusion. The presence of Chinese men in military and administrative documents reveals moments in which they were acknowledged, categorized, and incorporated—however imperfectly—into the structures of the state.


Conclusion


Military service during the Civil War made Chinese men visible within systems that both recognized and constrained them. Through enlistment records, service documentation, and pension files, these individuals entered bureaucratic frameworks that shaped how their identities were recorded and remembered. Their experiences demonstrate that recognition was not a fixed condition, but a process shaped by the interaction of race, institutions, and historical circumstance.


Sources and Further Reading



McClain, Charles J. In Search of Equality : The Chinese Struggle against Discrimination in Nineteenth-Century America. Edited by Charles J. McClain. Berkeley, CA: University of California Press, 1996. doi:10.1525/9780520917811.


Choy, Philip P, Lorraine Dong, and Marlon K Hom. Coming Man : 19th Century American Perceptions of the Chinese. First University of Washington Press paperback edition. Seattle: University of Washington Press, 1995.


McCunn, R.L. Chinese Yankee: A True Story from the Civil War. Design Enterprises of San Francisco, 2014. https://books.google.com/books?id=vgjcoQEACAAJ.

title: American Perceptions of Immigrants
text:
How were Chinese immigrants understood by the Americans around them during the Civil War era? Public perceptions of Chinese men were shaped not only by direct interaction, but by newspapers, popular discourse, and racialized assumptions that framed how their presence was interpreted within American society.


Public Discourse and Racial Assumptions


In the mid-nineteenth century, Chinese immigrants were often depicted through a limited set of racialized stereotypes. Newspapers, political rhetoric, and popular writing frequently portrayed Chinese individuals as foreign, unassimilable, or morally suspect. These representations shaped how Americans understood Chinese presence, even in places where direct interaction was limited.








“Chinaman’s Oath.” Milwaukee Daily Sentinel, January 15, 1859.



Such perceptions were not uniform, but they established a framework within which Chinese men were evaluated. Ideas about labor, gender roles, and cultural difference influenced how Chinese immigrants were viewed and how their actions were interpreted by broader society.




Political cartoon of 1886 called “Uncle Sam kicks out the Chinaman.” The George Dee Magic Washing Machine Company, 1886.



Perception and Military Service


Military service placed Chinese men in a position that could both reinforce and challenge existing assumptions. On one hand, enlistment demonstrated participation in a national cause, potentially complicating narratives that framed Chinese immigrants as outsiders. On the other hand, service did not necessarily alter the racial frameworks through which they were viewed.


Newspapers and public commentary rarely centered Chinese soldiers, and when they did, their presence was often filtered through existing expectations about race and difference. As a result, even acts of service could be interpreted in ways that reinforced rather than disrupted prevailing perceptions.


Perception and Its Consequences


Public perceptions had tangible effects on the lives of Chinese immigrants. Racialized assumptions influenced not only social attitudes but also legal and institutional responses, shaping the boundaries of inclusion and exclusion in American society. These perceptions contributed to the conditions under which Chinese men served, worked, and attempted to build lives in the United States.








“Printers Refusing to Work with a Chinaman.” Daily Evening Bulletin, August 5, 1861.



At the same time, the presence of Chinese soldiers complicates these narratives. Their participation in the Civil War demonstrates that, despite prevailing stereotypes, Chinese men were actively engaged in the political and military life of the nation.


Conclusion


American perceptions of Chinese immigrants during the Civil War era were shaped by a combination of racial assumptions, public discourse, and limited understanding. While these perceptions often constrained how Chinese men were viewed and treated, they did not fully define their experiences. By examining both representation and lived reality, this project reveals the gap between perception and participation, highlighting the complexity of Chinese presence in nineteenth-century America.


Sources and Further Reading



Lee, Erika. “The ‘Yellow Peril’ and Asian Exclusion in the Americas.” Pacific Historical Review 76, no. 4 (2007): 537–62. doi:10.1525/phr.2007.76.4.537.


Gyory, Andrew. Closing the Gate : Race, Politics, and the Chinese Exclusion Act. 1st ed. Chapel Hill: University of North Carolina Press, 1998.


Grant, Susan-Mary “When Is a Nation not a Nation? The Crisis of American Nationality in the Mid-Nineteenth Century,” Nations and Nationalism 2, no. 1 (1996): 105–29


Choy, Philip P, Lorraine Dong, and Marlon K Hom. Coming Man : 19th Century American Perceptions of the Chinese. First University of Washington Press paperback edition. Seattle: University of Washington Press, 1995.


Hirota, Hidetaka. “Introduction: Transpacific Connections in the Civil War Era.” The Journal of the Civil War Era 13, no. 4 (2023): 431–43.

title: About the Project
text:
About This Site
Although Chinese migrants have been present in the United States since the early 19th-century , their contributions to national conflicts—especially the Civil War—are rarely acknowledged in mainstream historical narratives. This omission not only perpetuates the stereotype of Chinese individuals as passive or apolitical immigrants but also distorts the historical record of U.S. military history and racial policy development. This research addresses a significant gap by documenting and analyzing Chinese participation in the Civil War.
While scholarship on African American, Native American, and even European immigrant soldiers has grown, Asian American military history remains underexplored—particularly in the pre-20th-century context. By situating Chinese service within the political, social, and legal frameworks of the Civil War era, this study expands our understanding of how military service intersected with racial hierarchies and citizenship policies. Moreover, this project contributes to Asian American studies by re-centering Chinese agency in foundational moments of U.S. history. It challenges the linear narrative that frames Asian Americans as only gaining political visibility in the 20th century and reinterprets the Civil War as a site of Asian American political engagement and contestation.


About the Researcher
The website is designed to make this research accessible to a wider audience. Advised by Dr. Paul Quigley, this project was created by Madison Smith, a graduate student in the History M.A. program at Virginia Tech. Her research focuses on nineteenth-century American legal history, immigration, race, and citizenship, with particular attention to the ways laws and institutions shaped the experiences of Asian immigrants in the United States.


Note From the Researcher
This project began as part of my Master’s portfolio during my time at Virginia Tech where it was first conceptualized as a paper. As I continued the research process, I realized that, while the National Park Service has a fantastic project dedicated to this field of study, there is little more than documentation of names. In attempting to better understand the lives of these soldiers, I began my own database to track each man and compile a more useful and condensed history that included scouring the archives for every bit of information I could find. It soon became clear that a paper was not the most sufficient output, but a website. This is the product, and is, by no means, complete.


An Ongoing Process
Research on Chinese Civil War soldiers is ongoing. New records continue to surface as historians explore archives and digitized collections. Recent scholarship has especially highlighted the contributions made by marginalized groups during the Civil War era, and this project represents one step in a broader effort to recover the lives of individuals whose stories have long been overlooked in traditional narratives of Civil War.
Should viewers have additional information to provide, please contact the researcher, Madison, at maddie111888@gmail.com.

title: Tracing Civil War Journeys
text:
This interactive map traces documented and approximate journey stops for soldiers and sailors in the dataset. It is designed as a public-facing research tool: readers can explore movement across enlistment points, transfers, receiving ships, discharge locations, and other recorded stops.
Please note that the lines connecting to each stop are not representative of the exact journey the individual might have taken, but rather a visualization of distance.



This first version of the map emphasizes documented locations and carefully standardized place names rather than speculative routes. Lines connect each person’s stops in order using stop_order.



Lines trace each recorded journey in sequence.
Point colors distinguish exact, approximate, and uncertain locations.
Line colors distinguish Army and Navy records.
Clicking a point opens source-based details for that stop.

title: John Hang
text:
John (Ah) Hang’s (Tong Kee Hang) life offers one of the more detailed and revealing stories of a Chinese immigrant who served during the American Civil War.







John Hang, 1911. Alex Jay, “John / William Hang,” The Blue, the Gray and the Chinese (blog), https://bluegraychinese.blogspot.com/search/label/John%20%2F%20William%20Hang.




Basic Information



Born: Canton, July 17, 1841


Service: Union Navy


Enlisted: July 24, 1863


Discharged: September 30, 1864



Early Life


Hang’s actual birth year and age was questioned during his entire life, but he alleged that he had been born in Canton, China, on July 17, 1841. He eventually made his way to the United States in 1857 at about 16 years of age. Prior to his service in the U.S. Hang claimed to work as a Steward on the vessel Shakespeare.


Military Service









John Hang, date unknown. “John/William Hang (Tong Kee Hang),” in “Honor & Duty: Chinese Servicemen in the American Civil War,” US Dandelion, https://usdandelion.com/archives/6192.




Hang enlisted on July 24, 1863, serving aboard the USS Albatross and USS Penguin. He worked as both a landsman and cabin steward, positions that placed him within the daily labor systems that sustained naval operations. In an interview given years via a pension record later, Hang explains that his name was written down as “John Ah Hang” when he enlisted, but that this was the Chinese way of pronouncing it.


Hang claims that, at the time, he did not know enough about English to remember the names of the officials on the boat, but he remembered exactly what duties he completed.




USS Albatross (1861-1865); Sketch by William M. C. Philbrick, depicting her off Mobile, Alabama, on 25 September 1863. Photo #: NH 57264-A; From the Private Papers of William M. C. Philbrick, Carpenter’s Mate, USS Portsmouth. U.S. Naval Historical Center Photograph



While on the Albatross, Hang assisted in blockading duty around Mobile Bay for about 8-9 months before transferring to the Penguin.


There, he acted as Cabin Steward. He recalled the time that a couple of men on the ship became very sick and were taken to the hospital, and although he did not know the name of the sickness, he was sure it was not yellow fever. While landsmen performed general ship duties, cabin stewards often served officers directly. Hang remained in service until his final discharge on September 30, 1864 at Boston, Massachusetts, surviving the war and transitioning into civilian life.




Postwar Life




After the war, Hang built a life in New York City. He worked as a tobacco merchant, operating businesses on Pearl Street and Mott Street, and later resided at the Soldiers’ and Sailors’ Home as he aged.




The Soldiers’ and Sailors’ Home. Wm. M. Clarke, The New York State Soldiers’ and Sailors’ Home: Bath, New York, lithograph, 1881–1888, The Huntington Library, Jay T. Last Collection, https://hdl.huntington.org/digital/collection/p16003coll4/id/1418.


His first application for a pension was successful, although there was an investigation held in 1908 after an author writing about the Chinese residents in New York requested an inquiry. This resulted in an investigator transcribing his interview with Hang in which he recounts his life story up until that point. His pension was resumed after this. His successful pension application demonstrates that he was able to secure federal recognition for his wartime service—something many immigrant veterans struggled to achieve.



Historical Significance




Yet Hang’s life also reveals the limits of that recognition. Despite his military service and long residence in the United States, he attempted to naturalize under the name William Hang and succeeded, however it was taken away for him shortly after. His experience reflects the broader exclusion of Chinese immigrants from American citizenship in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.


Hang’s personal life further illustrates his integration into American society. He married twice—first to Jennie Busch in Savannah, Georgia, in 1868, and later to Maggie Duffy in 1878. Both marriages connect him to diverse immigrant communities, highlighting the interconnected social worlds of port cities like New York and Savannah. Unfortunately both of his marriages ended with him widowed, and he never remarried nor had any children.


John Hang died in Staten Island, New York, on December 3rd, 1923.





Sources



“Tong Kee Hang”


“Historical Record of Chinese Americans”


“John/William Hang”

title: Chinese Civil War Soldiers
text:
In the nineteenth century, Chinese men fought in the American Civil War—yet their presence has largely remained absent from its historical narrative. Their lives survive only in fragments across enlistment records, census schedules, pension files, and scattered references in newspapers. This project reconstructs those lives, tracing how Chinese men participated in the war and what that participation reveals about race, citizenship, and belonging in the United States.


Through soldier profiles, thematic essays, and digital mapping, the project examines three interconnected questions. First, what did it mean for Chinese men to fight for a nation that did not fully recognize them as citizens? Second, how did military service place them within bureaucratic systems that recorded and classified their identities? And third, how were they perceived by the Americans around them, and how did those perceptions shape the possibilities available to them? Taken together, these perspectives reveal Civil War participation not as a simple marker of inclusion, but as part of an ongoing process of negotiation shaped by race, institutions, and public discourse.


This project builds on work preserved by the National Park Service and other archival institutions.

title: Robert Spicer
text:
Robert Spicer, date unknown. Chittendon, David. “Photos of Robert Spicer - Find a Grave Memorial.” Find a Grave, September 8, 2013. https://www.findagrave.com/memorial/116775306/robert-spicer/photo#view-photo=188068800. 



Basic Information



Born: Shanghai, 1842


Service: Union Navy


Enlisted: July 21, 1862


Discharged: July 19, 1863



Early Life


Robert Spicer was born in Shanghai, China, in 1842.
Newspaper accounts reported that he was brought to the United States in 1856 as a child by the wealthy sea-captain, Elihu Spicer, who purchased the boy from his parents in China for eight dollars. While the exact circumstances of this transaction remain difficult to verify, such arrangements were not uncommon in port communities like Mystic and New London, where sailors, merchants, and laborers regularly moved between Asia and the United States. Unfortunately, Spicer’s original Chinese name has been lost, but records show that he did adopt Capt. Spicer’s surname, and took “Robert” for his first. It was likely this coastal connection, as well as the fact that Captain Spicer himself became the captain of a Union steamship, that made enlistment in the Navy more accessible for him.
The 1860 census listed him as a seventeen-year-old laborer, showing that he began working before the outbreak of the conflict.


Military Service


Spicer eventually found himself serving in the Union Navy during the Civil War. He enlisted on July 21, 1862 in New London, Connecticut as a landsman aboard the USS Sabine, a Union vessel, and was discharged on July 19th, 1863.




U.S.S. Sabine, 1869. “NH 91722 USS Sabine, 1855-83.” Navy History and Heritage Command. https://www.history.navy.mil/our-collections/photography/numerical-list-of-images/nhhc-series/nh-series/NH-91000/NH-91722.html. 



Postwar Life


After his service, Spicer remained in Connecticut and continued working along the coast. On July 16, 1875, he married Alice Somers at St. Mark’s Church. An 1880 census lists his occupation as a fisherman, reflecting a life tied closely to maritime labor. Spicer also sought payment and recognition for his service, as in 1889, he applied for and received a federal pension.
According to a certificate later filed by his wife, he suffered for years from chronic illness, including fever, “ague”, and persistent diarrhea that she believed was brought on by his service. The couple lived in the coastal community of Noank, Connecticut for the remainder of their lives.
Alice Somers was born in 1850 in Ireland, and immigrated to the United States with her family when she was four years old. The couple did not have any children. Robert Spicer died on March 26, 1900, and newspapers remembered him as a well-known figure– nicknamed “Bob”– in the community and a respected veteran. His funeral was attended by the Grand Army of the Republic, the nation’s largest Union veteran’s association, of which Spicer was also a member. He is buried in Noank Cemetery. His wife, Alice Somers Spicer, would join him in his rest on February 24th, 1915.



Spicer’s Grave. Chittendon, David. “Photos of Robert Spicer - Find a Grave Memorial.” Find a Grave, September 8, 2013. https://www.findagrave.com/memorial/116775306/robert-spicer/photo#view-photo=188068800. 




Historical Significance


Newspaper accounts describing Spicer reveal how racial identity shaped American public perceptions of immigrant veterans. One obituary referred to him as a “naturalized Chinaman”, while another incorrectly described him as being of Japanese descent. These two descriptions alone demonstrate the uncertainty that surrounded immigrants in nineteenth-century America.
Even when discussing individuals like Spicer who lived in the United States for decades, journalists still frequently emphasized their racial identity. However, the same articles also remembered Spicer as a respected member of the community, and all fondly noted his nickname–”Bob.” He was described as being well-liked in fishing circles and honored by the Grand Army of the Republic. This recognition suggests that military service was still able to provide immigrants with some degree of legitimacy, even when the society around them viewed them as perpetual outsiders.
Through the limited documents we have, Spicer’s story can still be constructed to a fascinating degree. His life reflects the multi-facted realities faced by many immigrant veterans, and illustrates how global migration, wartime service, and local community intersected in the decades following the Civil War.


Sources



Naval enlistment record
Pension record


Newspaper references

“Robert Spicer’s Funeral” The Day, March 29, 1900, p. 3.
“The funeral of the late Robert Spicer, known to every one as”Bob.” was emnized at the Baptist church yesterday afternoon. The arrangements were charge of the Grand Army, of which ceased was a member. A large number friends attended who accepted this the opportunity to attest to the high esteem which they yield this departed citizen. C. Martin preached the funeral sermon and spoke most feelingly, paying just ute to the memory of one who had always lived an upright life during his many residence in this place. The interment took place in Noank cemetery.”
“Robert Spicer Passed Away While Putting on His Clothing” The Day, March 26, 1900, p. 3.
“Robert Spicer, a well known figure of place, dropped dead at his home on street, early this morning. He had no former signs of illness and had made rangements for a fishing trip today one of the local fishermen. He was for at the appointed hour but was partly dressed, lying on a sofa but was extinet. Mr. Spicer, more familiarly known”Bob,” was of Japanese descent and brought here from that country when small, by the late Capt. Elibu Spicer Mystic, who was then on a foreign It was so long ago that Bob has forgotten his mother tongue and spoke English language almost perfectly. original name was never known and correct age has always been a matter doubt, but when this country was he took the Spicer name with the name of Robert. He has always followed the water in ferent capacities but chiefly as steward was always well liked by his employers because of his faithfulness. He enlisted during the civil war and having served country honorably he received a small sion, which was his main support in latter years of his life “Bob” was a friend to every one and return every one was a friend to him. was quiet in his ways and liked by one and will be missed in fishing circles. He was a member in good standing of Grand Army post at Mystic, by which will probably be buried. He leaves a mourn his loss”
“Naturalized Chinaman Who Served in Civil War” The Journal, March 26, 1900, p. 1.
“Spicer was found dead in bed at his home in Noank early this morning. Heart failure is believed to have been the cause of death. Spicer, was a Chinaman and was brought to this country in 1856 by Captain Spicer, a millionaire shipowner and sea captain of this place, who purchased the boy from his parents in China. The amount involved in the transaction was $8. When the Civil war broke out the young man enlisted in the United States navy and served continuously until peace was restored. For many years Mr. Snider had enjoyed the rights of citizenship. He is survived by a widow.”

title: John Comfort
text:
Although the surviving record reveals only limited details about John Comfort’s personal life, enough evidence remains to sketch the outlines of his service and later life.


Basic Information



Born: China, potentially 1845


Service: Union Navy


Enlisted: September 27, 1864


Discharged: October 26, 1866



Early Life


Little is currently known about Comfort’s early life before his enlistment. Surviving records suggest that he was born in China, possibly around 1845, but they do not yet provide much detail about his family background, childhood, or migration to the United States. This absence is itself revealing, reflecting the fragmentary way Chinese lives often entered nineteenth-century American archives.


Military Service


John Comfort enlisted in the Union Navy on September 27, 1864, at the age of nineteen. He served for two years before being discharged on October 26, 1866. Records show that he served as a landsman aboard the U.S.S. North Carolina, the U.S.S. Seneca, and the U.S.S. Constellation.


Although the exact dates of his transfers between ships remain unclear, the histories of these vessels help place his service in context.



U.S.S. North Carolina. USS North Carolina from the Naval Historical Center in Washington, D.C.


By the time Comfort served aboard the U.S.S. North Carolina, the ship was functioning as a receiving ship rather than an active war vessel, suggesting that it may have served as an entry point in his naval experience.




The U.S.S. Seneca as she appeared at the Battle of Port Royal, 1887. British Library, “Digitised image from”Battles and Leaders of the Civil War, being for the most part contributions by Union and Confederate officers, based upon ‘the Century War Series.’,” Flickr Commons, https://www.flickr.com/photos/britishlibrary/11287950395/.



The U.S.S. Seneca, a wooden-hulled gunboat launched in 1861, served with the North Atlantic Blockading Squadron. During the period of Comfort’s service, the Seneca participated in major operations against Fort Fisher in late 1864 and early 1865, and later helped in the attack and capture of Fort Anderson in February 1865. If Comfort was aboard during this period, he would have been connected to some of the Navy’s important late-war campaigns along the Atlantic coast.




The U.S.S. Constellation. National Park Service, “Board the USS Constellation,” https://www.nps.gov/thingstodo/board-the-uss-constellation.htm.



Comfort also served aboard the U.S.S. Constellation, the last all-sail ship built by the United States Navy. Commissioned in 1855, the Constellation had already established a long service history by the time Comfort joined its crew. The ship is remembered both for its Civil War-era service and for its earlier role in suppressing the foreign slave trade.



Postwar Life



After the war, Comfort’s life appears to have taken him across the Pacific world. He married Au Kung Ling in Hong Kong in 1878. By 1895, he was living in New York City, suggesting that he had returned to the United States by the late nineteenth century. Together, John and Au Kung Ling had a daughter, Tai Kau, who was born on July 27, 1899. Comfort died on April 6, 1907.


Historical Significance


John Comfort’s story highlights both the possibilities and the limitations of the historical record for recovering Chinese participation in the Civil War. Like many of the men in this project, he survives only in scattered traces across enlistment records, family records, and later documentation. Yet even these fragments reveal important patterns. His naval service shows that Chinese-born men were present within Union military institutions, while his later life in Hong Kong and New York points to the transnational dimensions of Chinese experience in the nineteenth century. Comfort’s life therefore helps illuminate the broader connections among migration, military service, and belonging in this era.


Sources



“Comfort Families in America”


Weekly return of enlistments at Naval Rendezvous (“Enlistment Rendezvous”), Jan. 6, 1855-Aug. 8, 1891

title: The Dataset
text:
This project compiles a dataset of Chinese soldiers and sailors who served during the Civil War, drawing on military enlistment records, pension files, census data, and newspaper sources.
Previous scholarship has identified approximately 58 Chinese American soldiers and sailors who served during the Civil War. This project builds on that foundation by identifying additional individuals through expanded archival research, including pension files and federal census records, and bringing that number to 80.
Developed alongside the research and interpretive components of the site, the dataset brings together information drawn from a wide range of archival sources in order to document military service, movement, labor, and postwar life. For more about the researcher’s methodology, see Methodology.




Download the full dataset (CSV)

Download the full dataset (Excel)

The dataset is provided as a public resource for research, teaching, and further exploration.




The database includes individuals identified through enlistment records, pension files, naval documents, census data, and contemporary newspapers. Each entry represents a synthesis of available evidence rather than a single archival record.
Fields in the dataset may include:

Name

Alternate names and variant spellings

Birthplace

Service branch (Army or Navy)

Rank at enlistment and discharge

Ship or regiment

Enlistment and discharge dates

Occupation

Residence

Pension status

Notes

Source references

Where possible, entries trace individuals across multiple stages of life, from military service to postwar settlement. In many cases, however, the archival record remains incomplete.




This database is not a complete record of Chinese participation in the Civil War. Instead, it represents what can be recovered from an archive that was never designed to systematically document these individuals.

Because these individuals rarely appear in a single, cohesive record, the project draws on multiple source types to reconstruct their lives across military service, migration, and postwar experience.

title: Robert Spicer: A Sailor from Shanghai
text: Robert Spicer’s journey to the American Civil War began far from the battlefields of the United States…

title: Robert Spicer: A Sailor from Shanghai
text:
Why his story matters
Spicer’s experience reflects a broader theme explored in this project: how immigrants and minority soldiers used military service to claim recognition in a nation that often viewed them as outsiders.

title: Fighting for Belonging
text:
What did it mean for men who were not fully recognized as American citizens to fight in the nation’s most defining military conflict? For Chinese men in the Civil War era, military service did not resolve questions of exclusion, but it created new opportunities for visibility, negotiation, and belonging within American society.


Service and Exclusion


Chinese migrants were present in the United States in small but growing numbers prior to the Civil War, mostly along the West Coast but also in eastern port cities such as New York and Boston. By the 1860s, a limited number of Chinese men had entered maritime and labor networks that brought them into contact with Union military structures. Although their numbers remained small—scholars estimate between 150 and 300—their presence complicates assumptions about Chinese exclusion as a purely postwar phenomenon. In the decades following the war, however, these individuals and others like them became subject to increasingly restrictive immigration policies, culminating in the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882.


These individuals also occupied an uncertain legal and social position in the United States. They were present within the nation, but not fully incorporated into its political or civic framework. Military service therefore placed these men in a contradictory position: they contributed to the preservation of the Union while remaining outside the boundaries of formal citizenship.


This contradiction reflects broader tensions in Civil War-era America. In April 1862, the Confederacy implemented the first national conscription law, while the United States federal government followed with the Enrollment Act of 1863. These developments expanded the relationship between military service and citizenship, even as that relationship remained uneven and exclusionary.


Military Service as Negotiation


For Chinese men, enlistment in the Union Navy and Army created opportunities to engage with institutions that might otherwise have excluded them. Military service provided wages, structure, and a form of official recognition, even if that recognition did not translate into full legal inclusion.


Service could also generate records—enlistment papers, service histories, pension files—that made these men more legible to the state. In this sense, military participation was not only an act of labor or loyalty, but also a form of negotiation. Through service, Chinese men became part of bureaucratic systems that documented their presence and, in some cases, preserved their stories.


Individual Lives and Broader Patterns


The significance of military service becomes clearer when viewed through individual lives. The experience of Robert Spicer, for example, demonstrates how naval service could form part of a longer trajectory that included migration, labor, and postwar life in the United States. His service connected him to institutions that would later shape his claims to recognition and memory.


Similarly, the record of John (Ah) Hang illustrates how service generated documentation that extended beyond the war itself. Pension files, interviews, and other records created a paper trail that allows historians to reconstruct his life in greater detail than might otherwise be possible.


These individual cases reveal broader patterns. Military service did not erase racial exclusion, but it created conditions under which Chinese men could assert presence, build records, and participate—however unevenly—in the national story of the Civil War.


Belonging and Its Limits


Despite these possibilities, the relationship between service and belonging remained incomplete. Chinese men who served were not automatically granted citizenship, nor were they fully accepted within American society. The benefits of service were therefore limited and contingent, shaped by broader racial attitudes and legal restrictions.


At the same time, their participation complicates simple narratives of exclusion. By serving in the military, these men inserted themselves into one of the most significant national institutions of the nineteenth century. Their presence challenges assumptions about who could participate in the war and what forms of belonging were available to those on the margins.


Conclusion


Military service during the Civil War did not resolve the question of Chinese inclusion in the United States, but it reshaped it. Through enlistment, labor, and the records that followed, Chinese men created new forms of visibility within a society that often sought to exclude them. Their service reveals belonging not as a fixed status, but as an ongoing process of negotiation shaped by race, law, and historical circumstance.

title: Sources
text:
Pension Files
Pension records are among the richest sources in this project. Unlike enlistment records, which are largely administrative, pension files often contain:

Personal affidavits from veterans
Testimony from family members, shipmates, or community members
Medical evaluations and documentation of disability
Marriage and death records

These files extend beyond wartime service, allowing the reconstruction of postwar lives, including family formation, economic conditions, and long-term health. At the same time, they reflect the bureaucratic requirements of the federal government, as applicants were required to provide evidence in forms that aligned with state expectations.

Example: Antonio Dardell Pension File (27th Connecticut Infantry)
The pension file of Antonio Dardell illustrates the range of evidence pension records can contain. Dardell, who served in Company A of the 27th Connecticut Infantry, applied for a pension decades after his Civil War service. His file includes official identification forms, a formal declaration for pension, and supporting affidavit material, showing both the depth of personal information preserved in these records and the evidentiary burden placed on veterans seeking recognition. :contentReferenceoaicite:0






Why this source matters
These pages show how pension files moved from bureaucratic recordkeeping to personal testimony. Together, they document service, formal claims-making, and the human witnesses required to support recognition.








Claim sheet for Antonio Dardell’s pension application, identifying his Civil War service and file number.


Pension file of Antonio Dardell, Company A, 27th Connecticut Infantry, Record Group 15, National Archives.

Pension file of Antonio Dardell, Company A, 27th Connecticut Infantry, Record Group 15, National Archives.




Affidavit submitted in support of Dardell’s claim, demonstrating the role of witness testimony in verifying identity and service.

For another example of what pension records can reveal, see John Hang.



Census Records
Federal census data is used to trace individuals across time, particularly in the decades following the war. These records provide:

Occupations and economic status

Household composition

Residential patterns within port cities and coastal communities

Census data helps situate Chinese veterans within broader social and geographic contexts, revealing how military service intersected with labor, migration, and community formation.



Ship Logs and Maritime Records
Ship logs and naval documentation provide critical insight into the movements and labor structures of Chinese sailors. These sources include:

Crew lists and ship assignments

Records of voyages and ports of call

Notes on discipline, labor, and onboard conditions

Because many Chinese individuals entered military service through maritime labor networks, these records help connect Civil War service to broader transnational patterns of movement.



Newspapers and Public Discourse
Nineteenth-century newspapers are used to contextualize how Chinese individuals were represented in public discourse during and after the Civil War. These sources include:

Reports on military service and naval activity

Local coverage of Chinese communities

Editorials and commentary reflecting racial attitudes

While Chinese soldiers are rarely the central focus of these articles, newspapers provide insight into the broader cultural environment in which they lived and served. To see how this discourse affected an individual’s memory, see Robert Spicer.



Secondary Sources
In addition to archival materials, this project draws on a body of historical scholarship that provides context for understanding race, migration, and citizenship in the nineteenth-century United States.
Key works:
Arielli, Nir, and Collins, Bruce, eds. Transnational Soldiers: Foreign Military Enlistment in the Modern Era. Basingstoke, UK: Palgrave Macmillan UK, 2012. 
Bailey, Anne J. Invisible Southerners : Ethnicity in the Civil War. Athens: University of Georgia Press, 2006.
Black, Jeremy. War in the 19th Century, 1800-1914. Cambridge: Polity, 2009.
Blight, David W, and American Council of Learned Societies. Race and Reunion the Civil War in American Memory. Cambridge, Mass: Belknap Press of Harvard University Press, 2003.
Grant, Susan-Mary “When Is a Nation not a Nation? The Crisis of American Nationality in the Mid-Nineteenth Century,” Nations and Nationalism 2, no. 1 (1996): 105–29
Lee, Erika. At America’s Gates: Chinese Immigration during the Exclusion Era. Chapel Hill, NC: University of North Carolina Press, 2003.
Lew-Williams, Beth. The Chinese Must Go: Chinese, Exclusion, and the Making of the Alien in America. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 2018.
Salyer, Lucy E. Laws Harsh as Tigers: Chinese Immigrants and the Shaping of Modern Immigration Law. Chapel Hill, NC: University of North Carolina Press, 1995.
These works provide historical context and help situate the project within broader scholarly conversations, but the core of the analysis remains grounded in the archival record.



Bringing the Sources Together
No single source fully captures the experiences of Chinese Civil War participants. Instead, this project relies on the intersection of multiple record types to reconstruct individual lives. Military records establish service, pension files provide narrative depth, census data traces continuity, and newspapers reveal the broader cultural context.
Taken together, these sources allow for a more complete account of individuals who are otherwise only partially visible in the historical record.
